title: Premium 3D Board-Game Visual Spec — measured from Catan Universe and THE GAME OF LIFE 2
rules: CAMERA — Use a perspective camera at 40 degrees pitch with a 35 degree vertical FOV, never orthographic. Measured directly from catan_2.jpg: the sea-hex column pitch grows from 163px at the far edge of the board to 195px at the near edge, and hex apparent height/width climbs from 0.559 (centre row y=276) to 0.831 (y=766). Least-squares fit across six depth samples gives pitch 39.6 deg, focal 1720px at 1080p, vertical FOV 34.9 deg, RMS 0.022. An orthographic or fake-isometric camera cannot produce that gradient and is the single fastest way to look amateur.

CAMERA — Hold ONE fixed camera for the main board state; do not let the player orbit. catan_2.jpg, catan_3.jpg and catan_4.jpg are three different board layouts and three different game modes shot from an identical framing. The camera is the game's proscenium, not a toy.

CAMERA — Frame the board to fill roughly 66% of frame height and 65% of frame width, with the board centre sitting about 5% BELOW frame centre. In catan_2.jpg the board spans y=235..945 (centre y=590 against a frame centre of 540) because the player HUD owns the top of the screen. Bias the lookAt target upward so the composition balances against the HUD, rather than centring the board geometrically.

CAMERA — Add secondary framings per game beat, cross-faded rather than cut. THE GAME OF LIFE 2 changes camera per moment: life2_1.jpg is near-top-down (~60-70 deg) for the spin, life2_2.jpg is a low travel cam at ~18 deg pitch (horizon measured at y=194), life2_4.jpg is near eye-level at ~10 deg (horizon y=338) for the wedding cutscene. For a track-and-pawn game, hold the Catan-style 40 deg table view as home, and add a tighter ~55 deg dice/spin camera and a ~25 deg pawn-follow camera.

ENVIRONMENT — The board must sit inside a full-bleed environment that reaches every edge of the frame. There is no letterbox, no CSS gradient backdrop, no grey void anywhere in catan_2/3/4.jpg: the wooden table runs to all four edges and out of frame. In life2_2.jpg the world is a complete landscape with sky, sea, houses, lamps, benches and trees. The environment is what makes the board feel placed rather than floating.

ENVIRONMENT — Light the surround as a pool of light centred on the board, falling off to roughly 0.44 of centre luminance at the frame corners. Measured on the bare table wood in catan_2.jpg (8-bit luma): centre band x=400..1550 reads 124-126 at y=650; the mid-edges read 94-109; the top-left corner reads 55-76 and the bottom-right corner 55. Peak brightness sits at y~650, slightly below frame centre, i.e. on the board. This vignette does the framing job that a hobby demo tries to do with a border.

ENVIRONMENT — Put one or two defocused props at the frame edge to establish depth. catan_2.jpg and catan_3.jpg both carry a blurred vessel/horn silhouette in the top-left corner, out of focus and cropped by the frame. It costs one mesh and instantly reads as a photographed table rather than a render.

LIGHTING — Warm key, cool fill, and never crush the shadows. In life2_2.jpg lit grass reads #96C030 (luma 166) and the tree's cast shadow reads #476F26 (luma 97) — the shadow retains 58% of the lit value. Per-channel the shadow keeps only 48% of red but 84% of blue, so the fill is distinctly cool sky-bounce against a warm key. Shadows crushed toward black are the giveaway of a single unlit directional.

LIGHTING — Contact shadows must be tight and dark, not large and soft. In catan_2.jpg the magenta settlement at x=1055 transitions from piece side (#710954, y=510) to lit sand (#F2C375, y=516) in about 6px — the shadow is a hard, small pool directly under the piece footprint. Big blurry blobs read as a default three.js shadow map with too large a frustum.

MATERIALS — Board tiles are extruded slabs with visible side walls and inter-tile gaps, never a texture on a plane. In catan_2.jpg and the tile close-up, each hex shows a darker extruded rim and a bevelled sandy border, and the seams between tiles reveal the side geometry. Zero-thickness tiles are the clearest tell of a WebGL demo.

MATERIALS — Playing pieces read as injection-moulded glossy plastic: top faces about 30% brighter than side faces, plus a narrow specular streak along the top edge. Measured in catan_2.jpg on the magenta settlement — top face #980A76 (luma 48.0), side face #710954 (luma 36.6), ratio 0.76; the magenta road top catches a highlight up at #F14ABE against a base of #C21FC2. Use MeshStandardMaterial with roughness ~0.35 and a small environment map; never MeshBasicMaterial or MeshLambertMaterial.

MATERIALS — Board surfaces are matte and hand-painted; pieces are glossy. In catan_2.jpg the water hexes sample identically (#53809D) at both the far edge (y=300) and the near edge (y=880), meaning the tile faces are near-uniformly lit with almost no specular, while the plastic pieces carry strong directional shading. The contrast between matte terrain and shiny tokens is what separates the two layers visually.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — Keep roughly 80% of the frame free of UI. In catan_2.jpg the HUD occupies only the top 17% (player panels y=28..183), a 45px-wide left rail, a bottom-centred resource drawer and a bottom-right action cluster. In life2_1.jpg the player panel is 598x192 top-left and the prompt banner is 834x148 top-right; everything between is 3D.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — Player panels sit in a single row across the top, evenly pitched, one per player. Measured in catan_2.jpg: four panel units each 358px wide at a 448px pitch (18.6% and 23.3% of 1920), first panel starting at x=104, top inset 28px. This scales to any player count without reflowing the board.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — Encode player colour on at least five surfaces, not one dot. In catan_2.jpg each player's colour appears on the name plate (#A42423 red / #00638A blue / #BC7D1E gold / #9E299B purple), the portrait card background, the victory-point badge, the darkened stat pennants beneath, the hand-card counters, and the physical pieces on the board. Colour identity is a system, not a swatch.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — Indicate the active player with four redundant cues simultaneously. In catan_4.jpg Max's panel carries: a gold portrait frame (#E8A93C) where the inactive Jean's is neutral dark blue-grey, a 2px gold stroke running the length of the name pennant, a small gold chevron pointing down at the panel from above, and a dice glyph button that appears in the stats row only on the active turn. Inactive panels have none of these.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — The primary action control lives bottom-right, large, and glows. In catan_2.jpg the roll/end-turn button is a 75x75px gold button at 24px right / 26px bottom inset, wearing a warm amber halo that no other control has; the two dice (50x50px each) sit 62px above it. In life2_2.jpg the equivalent controls are 140px purple hexagons in the same corner. Never bury the primary action in a text button.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — A vertical icon rail on the left edge holds secondary/meta functions only. catan_2.jpg: eight 45x45px buttons at a 60px pitch running y=540..1000, inset 23px from the left, holding chat, emotes, log, stats, info, rules, settings and quit. Nothing that affects the game state lives there.

HUD ARCHITECTURE — Every UI element is a physical object: an opaque frame, an inner gradient face, and a drop shadow. Catan buttons (catan_2.jpg) have a 4-8px dark charcoal bezel (#3E3438) around a gold face that gradients #F5C63A to #E8862C. Name plates are pennants with a cut chevron tail. Hand-card counters physically overhang the bottom of the portrait card and are rotated a few degrees. In life2_2.jpg the buttons are hexagonal plastic tokens with a cream outer shell casting a shadow onto the board, and in life2_1.jpg the prompt banner hangs from two strings with visible grommets. There is not one flat translucent-black rectangle in any of the eight screenshots.

TYPOGRAPHY — Heavy weights, maximum contrast, always on a solid plate. Catan (catan_2.jpg): player names in bold humanist sans, white with a soft dark drop shadow, on a fully opaque coloured pennant. THE GAME OF LIFE 2 (life2_1.jpg): heavy rounded geometric sans, pure black on pure white plates, or pure white on saturated red. No mid-greys, no light weights, no text on a gradient anywhere.

TYPOGRAPHY — The only text permitted directly on the 3D scene is text baked into the geometry's own material. In catan_2.jpg the number tokens carry an old-style serif numeral (black, red for 6 and 8) with probability pips beneath, textured onto the token mesh so it takes the scene's perspective and lighting. Everything else — names, counts, prompts — sits on a plate. Screen-space or billboarded labels floating over the board are the classic failure.

TYPOGRAPHY — Dim what is zero. In the catan_2.jpg resource drawer, counts of 0 render in grey (#8A8A8A) with a desaturated icon, while non-zero counts are pure white with a full-colour icon. State is legible at a glance without reading a single digit.

LAYOUT — Vary corner radii by element class rather than applying one radius everywhere. Measured in catan_2.jpg: 4px on the name/stats plates, 10px on portrait cards, 12px on rail buttons, 14px on the resource drawer, 18px on the primary action button. life2_1.jpg runs 16px on stat plates, 18px on the name plate, 28px on the panel shell and 34px on the banner, plus hexagons for buttons.

LAYOUT — Place identity and prompt in opposite top corners. life2_1.jpg and life2_3.jpg both put the player panel top-left and the instruction banner ("Spin to move!", "Grow your family!") top-right, leaving the whole centre and lower two-thirds to the 3D scene.
antiPatterns: Orthographic or fake-isometric camera. Catan is measurably perspective — hex column pitch grows 163px to 195px front-to-back in catan_2.jpg, and hex h/w foreshortening runs 0.559 to 0.831. A parallel projection kills the sense that the board is a physical object on a table.

Translucent black HUD rectangles (rgba(0,0,0,0.4) plus white system font) floating over the render. Zero instances across all eight screenshots. Every plate in both games is opaque, coloured, framed and shadowed.

A CSS gradient, flat colour, or grey void behind the board. Catan runs a full-bleed wooden table to all four frame edges; Life 2 runs a complete landscape with sky and sea. Nothing in either game says 'the world stops here'.

Uniform exposure across the frame with no vignette. Catan's bare table reads luma 124-126 at the centre and 55 at the corners — a 0.44 ratio. Flat, evenly-lit surrounds are the single strongest 'WebGL demo' signal.

Shadows crushed toward black, or no shadows at all. Life 2's shadowed grass keeps 58% of lit luminance and shifts blue (retains 84% of blue but only 48% of red). A pure-black shadow means you have a directional light and no ambient/hemisphere fill.
Shadow map frustum sized to the whole scene, producing soft grey blobs. Catan's contact shadows resolve in ~6px under a piece. Fit the shadow camera tightly to the board and use a small PCF radius.
Zero-thickness board tiles — a texture painted on a plane. Catan hexes are extruded slabs with visible side walls, bevelled sandy rims and real gaps between them.

MeshBasicMaterial or MeshLambertMaterial on pieces, so tokens have no specular and no top/side differentiation. Catan pieces show a 0.76 side-to-top luminance ratio plus a specular streak on the top edge.
Player colour communicated by a single coloured dot or border. Catan encodes it on six surfaces: name plate, portrait background, VP badge, stat pennants, hand cards, and the pieces themselves.

Active player shown by one change (a brightness bump or a border). Catan uses four simultaneous cues: gold frame, gold plate stroke, a chevron above the panel, and a turn glyph that only exists on the active panel.
Primary action rendered as a text button, or placed anywhere other than bottom-right. Both games put it bottom-right at 75-140px with a glow or a raised plastic shell.

Screen-space or billboarded text labels drawn over the 3D scene. Catan's tile numerals are baked into the tile material so they take the scene's perspective and lighting; every other string sits on a plate.
Thin or light font weights, and mid-grey text. Both games use heavy or extra-heavy weights exclusively, at black-on-white or white-on-saturated contrast.
One corner radius applied to everything ('8px on all the things'). Catan spans 4px to 18px by element class; Life 2 spans 16px to 34px plus hexagons.
HUD laid out in fixed pixels so it explodes at 4K and vanishes on mobile. Both lay out proportionally — Catan's player panels are 18.6% of frame width each at a 23.3% pitch.
Emoji or a generic icon font for icons. Both games use custom chunky glyphs at a single stroke weight, in Catan's case a dark brown glyph (#8A4A15) recessed into a gold face.

A free-orbit camera the player has to manage, or conversely a single camera that never reacts to a game beat. Catan holds one authored framing; Life 2 authors a different framing per beat and transitions between them.
HUD covering more than about 20% of the frame. Catan leaves roughly 82% of the screen as pure 3D — top strip, thin left rail, bottom drawer, bottom-right cluster, nothing else.
concreteValues:
CAMERA (three.js, board radius R = 10 world units, 16:9)
--------------------------------------------------------
const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(35, 16/9, 0.5, 200); // 35 deg VERTICAL fov (measured 34.9)
// pitch 40 deg below horizontal (measured 39.6); distance = 3.09 * R
camera.position.set(0, 1.99 * R, 2.37 * R);   // = (0, 19.9, 23.7)
camera.lookAt(0, 0.117 * R, 0);               // = (0, 1.17, 0) -> puts board centre ~5% below frame centre
// Horizontal FOV at 16:9 = 58.3 deg. Focal equivalent = 1720px at 1080p height.
// Secondary framings (Life 2 pattern), cross-fade 500ms cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1):
//   spin/dice cam : fov 40, pitch 58 deg, distance 1.6 * R
//   pawn-follow   : fov 50, pitch 24 deg, distance 2.2 * R, horizon visible at 18% frame height
//   cutscene      : fov 45, pitch 10 deg, near eye level

LIGHTING (three.js, renderer.toneMapping = ACESFilmicToneMapping, toneMappingExposure = 1.05)
--------------------------------------------------------
const hemi = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xFFF6E6, 0x6E3F1E, 0.55);           // warm sky / warm table bounce

const key = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xFFF1D6, 1.35);                     // ~4800K warm white
key.position.set(-0.8 * R, 1.8 * R, 0.6 * R);                               // upper-left, behind-ish camera
key.castShadow = true;

const fill = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0x9FC6EA, 0.35);                    // ~7800K cool sky fill, NO shadow
fill.position.set(1.0 * R, 0.8 * R, -0.6 * R);

const rim  = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xFFC98A, 0.50);                    // ~3200K warm rim, NO shadow
rim.position.set(0, 0.6 * R, -1.4 * R);

// Target ratio: shadowed surface must retain 0.58 of lit luminance (measured, life2_2.jpg),
// with blue retaining 0.84 and red only 0.48 -> shadows read cool, never black.

SHADOWS
--------------------------------------------------------
renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true;
renderer.shadowMap.type = THREE.PCFSoftShadowMap;
key.shadow.mapSize.set(2048, 2048);
key.shadow.camera.left = -1.15 * R;  key.shadow.camera.right =  1.15 * R;
key.shadow.camera.top  =  1.15 * R;  key.shadow.camera.bottom = -1.15 * R;
key.shadow.camera.near = 1;          key.shadow.camera.far   = 6 * R;
key.shadow.bias = -0.0005;
key.shadow.normalBias = 0.02;
key.shadow.radius = 3;               // tight: contact shadow resolves in ~6px at 1080p

POST
--------------------------------------------------------
// Vignette: radial, centre at (0.50, 0.58) of the viewport (peak brightness measured at y=650/1080).
// Falloff -> 0.70 of centre at mid-edges, 0.44 at corners. Measured luma: centre 124-126, edge 94-109, corner 55.
vignette: { offset: 0.92, darkness: 1.15, centreY: 0.58 }
// No bloom on the board. Glow only on the primary action control (see HUD).
// One or two defocused props cropped at a frame corner (catan_2/3 top-left) instead of a global DOF pass.

--------------------------------------------------------
Board tile (matte, hand-painted):  MeshStandardMaterial { roughness: 0.85, metalness: 0.0, envMapIntensity: 0.15 }

notes:
METHOD — Every number above is measured from the supplied files, not estimated. Camera pitch and FOV come from segmenting the 18 sea hexes in catan_2.jpg (connected-component analysis on the water colour #53809D), measuring each one's apparent height/width against its screen row, and least-squares fitting a pinhole model. The hexes are pointy-top (confirmed: four hexes at y0=234 share an identical top edge with a column pitch equal to their width, and the next row is offset by half a hex), giving a flat-on h/w of 1.155. Fit: pitch 39.6 deg, focal 1720px, vertical FOV 34.9 deg, RMS 0.022 across six depth bands. Vignette, shadow ratios, panel dimensions and all hex codes come from pixel sampling and run-length edge scans of the same files.

THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING — Every UI element is a physical object lit by the same world as the board, and nothing is ever drawn flat onto the render. In Catan every button carries a 4-8px dark bezel around a gradient face; name plates are pennants with cut chevron tails; the hand cards physically overhang and are rotated a few degrees; the dice are meshes on the table, not sprites. In Life 2 the buttons are cream-shelled plastic hexagons lying on the board casting their own shadows, and the instruction banner hangs from two strings with visible grommets. Across all eight screenshots there is not one translucent black rectangle with white text on it. A hobby WebGL board game is almost always identifiable in under a second by exactly that: a beautiful 3D scene with a flat CSS overlay bolted on top. The second-order version of the same principle is the pool of light: the Catan table is 2.3x brighter at the board than at the frame corners, so the composition frames itself.

STRUCTURAL NOTE FOR A TRACK-AND-PAWN GAME — Life 2 is the closer structural reference but Catan is the better quality target, and the two disagree in one place worth deciding deliberately. Life 2 uses a low travel camera with the horizon in frame (life2_2.jpg, horizon at y=194) because the pleasure is the journey; Catan uses a high table camera with no horizon because the pleasure is the board state. The recommendation is Catan's 40 deg table camera as home state (it reads more premium and keeps the whole board legible) with Life 2's beat-driven secondary cameras layered on for dice, movement and events — but the low camera should always return home, and it should cross-fade rather than cut.

CONFIDENCE — Camera pitch, FOV, all hex codes, all HUD dimensions and the shadow luminance ratio are directly measured and high-confidence. The three.js light intensities are derived (inverted from the measured 0.58 shadow-to-lit ratio and the per-channel warm/cool split) rather than read off, so treat them as a calibrated starting point and tune against a screenshot comparison. The Life 2 FOV figures are the least precise, since its low-poly untextured surfaces do not give clean foreshortening samples; they are bracketed from the horizon row, so pitch is solid to within a few degrees but FOV is a range (roughly 50-60 deg vertical).

CONTENT NOTE — catan_1.jpg is the Steam store header artwork (the CATAN UNIVERSE logo on a sunset landscape), not a gameplay capture, so no camera, HUD or material observations are drawn from it. life2_4.jpg is a cutscene rather than a board state, so it contributes only the low cutscene camera angle and confirmation that the HUD is fully hidden during cinematic moments — which is itself a rule worth adopting.
